paras: The attempted lynching at Duluth, Georgia, was a failed effort in June 1888 by citizens in and near Duluth to take an unnamed Black man from officers and lynch him after he was accused of attempting to rape a girl of about ten. After a crowd of 100 was reported to be coming for him at Lawrenceville, the sheriff obtained a judge's order and moved him to the jail at Monroe. Georgia papers carried the episode as a brief state-news item.

According to the Atlanta report, the man met a daughter of George Lowe, about ten years old, on the road to Duluth, asked her the way to a house, and persuaded her to walk part of the way with him along a settlement road through the woods. Out of sight of the main road he was said to have thrown her to the ground, then to have fled when her screams drew farm hands from a nearby field. The girl was reported to have a bruised neck but to be otherwise unhurt, and she was said to have been carrying water to the hands in her father's field.

After his capture the man was locked in the depot at Duluth and guarded by citizens and officers until a train arrived and he was put aboard. W. F. Brewer, a justice of the peace at Duluth, committed him for assault with intent to commit rape, and on Tuesday night, 12 June, the Duluth bailiff W. E. Johnson delivered him to the sheriff at Lawrenceville. The Savannah Morning News reported that a number of citizens in and near Duluth had tried "to get him from the officers with the purpose of lynching him, but they failed," a claim it attributed only to report.

That same night word reached Lawrenceville that a crowd of 100 was coming to take him for the same purpose. Acting on the report, the sheriff obtained an order from Judge Hutchins to remove the prisoner to another county for safe keeping, and he was carried to the jail at Monroe. The Atlanta account stated that he would have been "lynched had he not been removed."
The man's name does not appear in the coverage, and no report of a trial or its outcome was found. No arrests or official action against the would-be lynchers were reported.

The Savannah Morning News ran the story on 15 June 1888 in its "Georgia and Florida" column of state news, under a headline line reading "Lynchers Anxious to Get a Negro Flend Who Lived at Duluth." Its paragraph presented the accusation as fact and the lynching attempt without comment, beside an Irwin County item in which neighbors threatened to lynch a wounded Black man.

The Weekly Constitution of Atlanta printed a longer version on 19 June in its "Through Dixie" roundup, sharing much of the Savannah wording but adding the details of the alleged assault. It called the accused "the flend" and "the brute" and closed with the prediction that "He will get justice meted out to him without mercy when his trial is had." Neither paper named the accused man or the girl.

reader.title: Attempted lynching at Duluth, Georgia (1888)
bases: Citizens near Duluth reportedly tried to take an accused Black man from officers to lynch him and a crowd was reported coming to Lawrenceville for the same purpose, an attempted lynching that failed (A1, A2, A4).

No one was killed: the attempt to take the man from officers failed and he was moved to Monroe jail (A1, A4). The would-be lynchers acted on an accusation of attempted rape, and their number is given only as 'a number of citizens' and a reported crowd of 100 (A1).
The Savannah and Atlanta paragraphs share much of their wording and appear to derive from one original report, and the attempt itself is given in A1 only as 'it is reported' (A1, A3, A4).

accounts.label: Georgia state-news report (Savannah)
accounts.gist: Citizens in and near Duluth, 'it is reported', tried to get the man from officers to lynch him but failed; a reported crowd of 100 led the sheriff to move him to Monroe jail.

accounts.label: Atlanta weekly roundup
accounts.gist: Describes the alleged assault in detail and says the man was guarded in the Duluth depot by citizens and officers until put on the train, and would have been lynched had he not been removed.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News ran the item as a paragraph in its 'Georgia and Florida' column under the headline phrase 'Lynchers Anxious to Get a Negro Flend Who Lived at Duluth', presenting the accusation as fact and the lynching attempt without comment.

The Weekly Constitution called the accused 'the flend' and 'the brute' and wrote that 'He will get justice meted out to him without mercy when his trial is had', while reporting that removal had prevented a lynching.

record_check.dossier: No county is named in the coverage; the place evidence is Duluth, a justice there, and the sheriff at Lawrenceville.

record_check.record: said to have committed a fiendish outrage
record_check.dossier: Accused of assault with intent to commit rape on a girl of about 10, a daughter of George Lowe; 'fiend' appears only in headline and characterization.
The targeted man was described as 'a negro man' (Black).
Also carried in the Weekly Constitution (Atlanta), 19 June 1888, with fuller detail.
12 June 1888 is the Tuesday night the man was delivered to the Lawrenceville sheriff and the crowd was reported coming; the Duluth attempt may have been earlier, date not given.

info: The accused was delivered to the sheriff at Lawrenceville on a Tuesday night, which by the 15 June (Friday) issue was 12 June 1888; the date of the alleged assault and of the seizure attempt is not given.
Duluth, Georgia, with the threatened crowd reported coming to Lawrenceville; the man was moved to the jail at Monroe.
An unnamed Black man ('a negro man') targeted by the would-be lynchers; the alleged victim of the assault was an unnamed daughter of George Lowe, about 10 years old.
Accused of an assault with intent to commit rape on a girl of about 10 he met on the road to Duluth.
'A number of citizens in and near Duluth', reportedly; later a reported crowd of 100 said to be coming to Lawrenceville.
The man was held at Monroe jail awaiting trial; no report of a trial or its outcome was found.
